1:1:
Ch. i. 1–18. The Prologue. THE ETERNAL WORD OF GOD, THE SOURCE OF ALL EXISTENCE, LIFE, AND LIGHT, BECAME FLESH, DWELT AMONG US, WAS WITNESSED TO BY JOHN, REJECTED BY HIS OWN PEOPLE, BUT RECEIVED BY SOME, WHO HAD POWER GIVEN THEM TO BECOME THE SONS OF GOD. HE WAS THE PERFECTION AND END OF GOD'S REVELATION OF HIMSELF; WHICH WAS PARTIALLY MADE IN THE LAW, BUT FULLY DECLARED IN JESUS CHRIST.

vv. 1–5. The eternal pre-existence of the Logos; his personal distinctness, but essential unity with God. His working in creation and in the enlightening of men before his manifestation in the flesh; his non-apprehension by them.

1. ἐν ἀρχῇ = πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι (ch. xvii. 5). The expression is indefinite, and must be interpreted relatively to the matter spoken of: here it is the beginning of all things, by reason of πάντα δι᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο (ver. 3). These words, if they do not assert, at least imply the eternal præ-existence of the Divine Word. For ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν is not said of an act done ἐν ἀρχῇ (as in Gen. i. 1), but of a state existing ἐν ἀρχῇ, and therefore without beginning itself.

ἦν is not equivalent to ἔστιν, as Euthymius supposed. The existence of an enduring and unlimited state of being, implied in ἦν, is contrasted with ἐγένετο in ver. 3, and especially in ver. 14.

καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν. The usage of πρός here (chez, 'with') is borne out by the references. Basil remarks that John says πρὸς τὸν θεόν, not ἐν τῷ θεῷ, that he might set forth the distinct personality of the Word (ἵνα τὸ ἰδιάζον τῆς ὑποστάσεως παραστήσῃ). Both the inner substantial union and the distinct personality of the Logos are here asserted.

καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. As regards the form of the sentence, it is strictly parallel with πνεῦμα ὁ θεός (ch. iv. 24). Had John intended to say 'God was the Word,' what meaning could this have conveyed? None other than a contradiction to his last assertion, by which he had distinguished God from the Word. The omission of the article before θεός is not mere usage: ὁ λόγος θεός would give a sense liable to similar objections and destroy the idea of the Logos altogether. θεός must be taken as implying God in substance and essence — not ὁ θεός the Father in Person, but the divine essence. It does not mean θεῖος, nor is it to be rendered 'a god,' but — as in σὰρξ ἐγένετο where σάρξ expresses the state into which the Word entered — so in θεὸς ἦν, θεός expresses that essence which was His from eternity. The Logos was from eternity — was with God the Father — and was Himself God.
1:2: 2. In order to direct the mind to the difference (in unity) between the Logos and θεός, John recalls the reader's attention to the two first clauses of ver. 1, which he now combines, in order to pass on to the creative work, which distinctly belongs to the Logos. This verse also fixes the reference of αὐτοῦ in ver. 3, which might otherwise, after the mention of θεός, have seemed ambiguous.
1:3:
3. πάντα = τὰ πάντα (1 Cor. viii. 6: Col. i. 16), ὁ κόσμος (ver. 10). The parallelism of itself refutes the Socinian interpretation of πάντα as 'all Christian graces and virtues.' Olshausen observes that we never read in Scripture that 'Christ made the world,' but always that the Father made the world through the Son, or the world was made by the Father through the Son: because the Son never works of Himself but always as the revelation of the Father.

χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἕν. This addition is not merely a Hebraistic parallelism, but a distinct denial of the eternity and uncreatedness of matter as held by the Gnostics. They set matter, as a separate existence, over against God, and made it the origin of evil: but John excludes any such notion. Nothing was made without Him; all matter — and implicitly evil itself, in the deep and inscrutable purposes of creation — δι᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο.
1:4: 4. ζωή is not merely 'spiritual life,' nor 'the recovery of blessedness' (Tholuck, Kuinoel): the Logos is the source of all life to the creature, not ultimately but mediately (see ch. v. 26: 1 John v. 11). καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων — this is not to be understood of the teaching of the Incarnate Logos, but of the enlightening and life-sustaining influence of the eternal Son of God, in Whom was life. In the material world, light is the condition of life, and without it life degenerates and expires: so also in the spiritual world, the life which is in Him is to the creature the very condition of all development and furtherance of the life of the spirit. All knowledge, all purity, all love, all happiness, spring up and grow from this life, which is the light to them all. It is not φῶς but τὸ φῶς, because this is the only true light (see ver. 9, also 1 John i. 5).
1:5:
5. As light and life are closely connected ideas, so are death and darkness. The whole world lying in death and in darkness is the σκοτία here spoken of — not merely 'the darkened' (Eph. iv. 18), but the whole mass, with the sole exception of ὅσοι ἔλαβον αὐτόν (ver. 12; compare ch. iii. 19: 1 John v. 19).

τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει — φαίνει is not merely the historical present, but describes the whole process of the light of life in the Eternal Word shining in this evil and dark world: both by the OT revelations, and (see ch. x. 16; xi. 52) by all the scattered fragments of light glittering among the thick darkness of heathendom.

καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν — the darkness comprehended (understood, apprehended) it not. The other interpretation, 'overtook' or 'overcame,' is unobjectionable as to lexical usage (ch. xii. 35: Mark ix. 18), but yields no sense in the context. John states here as a general fact what he afterwards states of the appearance of the Incarnate Word to His own people (ver. 11). The sentences are strictly parallel: τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει ‖ εἰς τὰ ἴδια ἦλθεν, and ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν ‖ οἱ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν οὐ παρέλαβον.
1:6:
vv. 6–18. The manifestation and working of the Divine Word, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, incarnate in our flesh.

6. The Evangelist now passes to the historic manifestation of the Word. He announces briefly in these verses (6–7) what he afterwards narrates in detail (vv. 19–36). ἐγένετο — not ἦν as in ver. 1 — is the ordinary opening of an historical period (see Luke i. 5). There was a man sent, &c. In ἀπεσταλμένος παρὰ θεοῦ there is possibly a reference to Mal. iii. 1.
1:7: 7. εἰς μαρτυρίαν = not 'for a witness' (E.V.) but 'for witness, for the purpose of bearing witness.' ἵνα μαρτ. κ.τ.λ. is an expansion of εἰς μαρτ. The subject of his testimony was to be the Light, and the aim of it that all might believe δι᾽ αὐτοῦ — through him, i.e. through John, not through the Light, which would confuse the whole sense.
1:8: 8. John was himself ὁ λύχνος ὁ καιόμενος καὶ φαίνων (ch. v. 35) — not lumen illuminans but lumen illuminatum — a derived and reflected light, not the original and archetypal Light itself.
1:9:
9. ἀληθινόν (see refs.) in this connexion imports 'original, archetypal,' and is used of the true genuine sources and patterns of which we find here below only fragmentary imitations and derivations. Such an original was the Light here spoken of; John was only a derived light.

The construction of this verse has been much disputed. ἐρχόμενον εἰς τὸν κόσμον belongs to τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινόν, not to ἄνθρωπον. The former construction (of most ancient commentators and the E.V.) can only be defended by a Rabbinical usage in which πάντα ἄνθρωπον means 'all men'; but it is very questionable whether John ever speaks thus, and in any case the sentence would be but a less forcible repetition of ver. 4. It is the Light itself that was coming into the world.
1:10: 10. ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἦν — He was in the world. ὁ κόσμος δι᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο — the world was made by Him. καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτὸν οὐκ ἔγνω — and yet the world knew Him not. The three members form a climax: He was in the world (and therefore the world should have known Him), and the world was made by Him (much more then should it have known Him), and the world knew Him not. The καί is not connective but adversative ('and yet'). αὐτόν, not αὐτό, because though κόσμος has been the subject, yet the δι᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο brings in again the creative Logos, who is the Light.
1:11: 11. τὰ ἴδια here cannot well mean the world in general, nor οἱ ἴδιοι mankind: abundance of passages bear out the meaning which makes τὰ ἴδια His own inheritance or possession, i.e. Judæa; and οἱ ἴδιοι, the Jews. Compare especially the parable Matt. xxi. 33 ff. And thus ἦλθεν forms a nearer step in the approach to the declaration in ver. 14. He came to His own. οἱ δὲ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν οὐ παρέλαβον — παρέλαβον expresses the personal assumption of another to oneself as friend or companion.
1:12:
12. The ὅσοι primarily refers to the ἐκλογή among the Jews just spoken of, but also, by implication, the ἐκλογή in all the world. ἔλαβον = παρέλαβον above — as many as recognized Him as that which He was, the Word of God and Light of men.

ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα θεοῦ γενέσθαι. ἐξουσίαν is not merely capability (Lücke), still less privilege or prerogative (Chrysostom), but power (De Wette), involving all the actions and states needful to their so becoming, and removing all the obstacles in their way, e.g. the wrath of God and the guilt of sin. τέκνα θεοῦ is more comprehensive than υἱοὶ θεοῦ: the latter brings out chiefly adoption and hope of inheritance (Rom. viii. 14 ff.), whereas the former involves the whole generation and process of our life in the Spirit, as being from and of God, and consequently our likeness to God, walking in light as He is in light (1 John i. 5–7).
1:13: 13. The Jews grounded their claim to be children of God on their descent from Abraham. John here negatives any such claim. It is to be noticed that the conjunctions are not the merely disjunctive οὔτε...οὔτε, which would range the clauses as co-ordinate, but οὐδέ...οὐδέ, which rise in climax from one to another — not of blood, nor yet of the will of the flesh, nor yet of the will of man, but of God. Euthymius: having said 'not of blood,' he added more plainly 'not of the will of the flesh,' then explained this yet more fully by adding 'not of the will of man'; for blood and flesh constitute the man.
1:14:
14. σὰρξ ἐγένετο — became flesh: the most general expression of the great truth that He became man. He became that of which man in the body is compounded. The simplicity of this expression is no doubt directed against the Docetæ of the Apostle's time, who maintained that the Word only apparently took human nature. Therefore he says σὰρξ ἐγένετο, absolutely and literally became flesh.

ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν — 'sojourned' or 'tabernacled' among us. There is no reference to the flesh being the tabernacle of the Spirit; the word is one technically used in Scripture to import the dwelling of God among men (see Levit. xxvi. 11, 12: Ezek. xliii. 7: Sir. xxiv. 8).

καὶ ἐθεασάμεθα τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ — the Apostle's testimony as such (Acts i. 21). This glory was seen in the disciples' whole converse with the Lord, in His teaching and His suffering — and notably at the Transfiguration, to which ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός especially refers.

On ὡς, Chrysostom remarks (Hom. xii. in Joh.): not of comparison or similitude, but of confirmation and certain definition — 'we saw a glory such as it was fitting and natural that an only-begotten Son of the King of all should have.' μονογενής applied to Christ is peculiar to John (see refs.). It refers to and contrasts with the τέκνα τοῦ θεοῦ in vv. 12, 13: they receive their divine birth by faith in Him and through Him; but He is the μονογενής of the Father in the higher sense, in which He is γεγεννηκώς, the Son of God.

πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας — setting out the two sides of the divine manifestation in Christ: χάρις as the result of Love to mankind — ἀλήθεια (see refs. and ch. xiv. 6) as the unity, purity, and light of His own Character. These are not to be reduced to one idea by taking them as a hendiadys for 'true grace': such shallow explanations cover over the depths of Scripture.
1:15:
15. The testimony of John, so important as being the fulfilment of the very object for which he was ἀπεσταλμένος παρὰ θεοῦ, is ranged in this prologue parallel with the assertions of the Evangelist himself. This verse does not interrupt the train of thought, but confirms by this important testimony the assertion ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, showing that John bore witness to His præ-existence.

μαρτυρεῖ (present, for solemnity) — as part of the testimony still subsisting. κέκραγεν (perfect, in sense present): 'hath cried, so that the voice is still sounding' (Bengel — clamat Johannes cum fiducia et gaudio). The form of the words suggests that the Baptist had uttered these words in the power of the Spirit before he saw and recognized Jesus in the flesh; then on doing so, he exclaimed, 'This was He of whom I said...'

ὅτι πρῶτός μου ἦν — the only sense these words will bear: 'because He was (not ἐγένετο but ἦν, as in ver. 1) before me' — He existed, was in being, before me. An assertion of eternal pre-existence. The Baptist was divinely raised up and commissioned, and full of the Holy Ghost: his declarations were not merely conclusions reached by natural means, but inspirations and revelations of the Spirit.
1:16:
16. τὸ πλήρωμα is that of which He was πλήρης in ver. 14, and is not connected with the Gnostic pleroma at all. ἡμεῖς πάντες — all who believe on Him (ver. 12). ἐλάβομεν, καί — 'received, and that...' our relation to Him has been that of recipients out of His fulness, and the thing received has been grace.

χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος — the preposition ἀντί is properly used of anything which supersedes another or occupies its place. We have received continual accessions of grace; new grace coming upon and superseding the former. Thus Philo of God's grace: 'the first graces he withholds and keeps in store, and in their place gives other new ones, and third in place of second, and always new in place of older' (Mangey, i. 254).
1:17:
17. The connexion: we received from His fulness continual additions of grace, because that fulness is not like the law — a positive enactment, finite and circumscribed, of which it could be said that it ἐδόθη — but the bringing in of grace and truth, which ἐγένετο by Jesus Christ.

ἐδόθη and ἐγένετο are to be distinguished: 'Moses' law is not his own; Christ's grace and truth are His own' (Bengel: Mosis non sua est lex; Christi sua est gratia et veritas). The law was a positive enactment, given through Moses as a servant; but grace and truth came into being through Jesus Christ as its Author, whose own they are. Bengel truly observes: 'No philosopher puts words so accurately and observes their difference so carefully as John, especially in this chapter.'
1:18:
18. The connexion: Moses could not give out of the πλήρωμα of grace and truth, for he had no immediate sight of God, and no man can have; there is but One who can ἐξηγεῖσθαι θεόν — the μονογενὴς υἱός, who abides in the bosom of the Father.

θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακεν πώποτε — the sight of God here meant is not only bodily sight (though of that it is also true, Exod. xxxiii. 20: 1 Tim. vi. 16), but intuitive and infallible knowledge, which enables Him who has it to declare the nature and will of God (see ch. iii. 11; vi. 46; xiv. 7).

ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός — the expression must not be understood as merely referring to the custom of reclining in the bosom at table (ch. xiii. 23): it signifies, as Chrysostom observes, συγγένεια καὶ ἑνότης τῆς οὐσίας — kindred and unity of essence — derived from the intimate union of children and parents. The present participle (ὁ ὤν) signifies essential truth, without particular regard to time. εἰς is not 'put for' ἐν: it is a carrying on of the thought of ver. 1 (πρὸς τὸν θεόν), a pregnant construction involving in it the begetting of the Son and His being the Logos of the Father.

ἐκεῖνος ἐξηγήσατο — He, and none else. ἐξηγεῖσθαι and its cognates are technical terms for the declaration of divine matters (compare Wetstein's collection of passages). The object to be supplied is most likely αὐτόν, i.e. τὸν θεόν.

As to the reading: the great majority of the Fathers (Tertullian, Hippolytus, the Antiochene Synodical Epistle, Eusebius, Athanasius, Hilary, and apparently all Latin Fathers) read ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός. The reading μονογενὴς θεός, found in some important manuscripts (including B, C¹, L, N, 33), is adopted by Tischendorf but is far less strongly supported among the Fathers. Both ancient interpretation and the sense of the passage incline to υἱός.
1:19:
vv. 19–28. The first witness borne by John to Jesus: before the deputation from the Sanhedrim.

19. αὕτη is the predicate, ἡ μαρτυρία the subject. So very frequently in St. John, where the mistake is commonly made of supposing the demonstrative pronoun to be the subject, whereas it is ever the predicate of identification.

οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι — John alone of the Evangelists uses this expression, principally to designate the chiefs of the Jewish people, the members of the Sanhedrim. The usage is confirmatory of the belief that the Gospel was written after the Jews had ceased to be politically a nation, and among Gentiles, the author himself contemplating Gentiles as his readers.

ἀπέστειλαν ἐξ Ἱεροσολύμων ἱερεῖς καὶ Λευΐτας — a formal deputation; priests and Levites, the two classes employed in the service of the temple (Josh. iii. 3), sent officially to enquire into the pretensions of the new Teacher, who had collected such multitudes (Matt. iii. 5) and awakened popular expectation that he was the Messiah (Luke iii. 15).
1:20: 20. ὡμολόγησεν καὶ οὐκ ἠρνήσατο — he openly and formally confessed. This emphatic notice seems to be introduced not to remove too high an estimate of John, but rather to show the importance of his testimony, which was so publicly and officially delivered. He confessed that the Messiah was come, and deprecated any higher claim for himself.
1:21:
21. Ἡλίας εἶ; The whole appearance of John reminded them of Elijah (see Matt. iii. 4; 2 Kings i. 8). Besides, his announcement that the Kingdom of God was at hand naturally led them to the prophecy of Mal. iv. 5. The deputation asked the question in a mistaken and superstitious sense, meaning Elijah bodily come down from heaven, who was expected to forerun and anoint the Messiah. In this sense John was not Elijah; nor indeed in any other sense — but only (Luke i. 17) ἐν πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει Ἡλίου.

ὁ προφήτης εἶ σύ; From the prophecy of Moses (Deut. xviii. 15, 18) the Jews expected some particular prophet to arise, distinct from the Messiah, whose coming was intimately connected with that of the Messiah Himself (see ch. vii. 40, 41). This John was not: and he therefore answers this also in the negative.
1:22: 22. Note — they ever ask about his person; he ever refers them to his office. He is no one — a voice merely: it is the work of God, the testimony to Christ, which is everything. So the formalist in the church ever asks 'Who is he?' while the witness for Christ only exalts and cares for Christ's work.
1:23: 23. The words of Isa. xl. 3, which by the other Evangelists are spoken of John as the fulfilment of prophecy, appear from this place to have been first so used by the Baptist himself. They introduce the great closing section of Isaiah's prophecy (ch. xl.–lxvi.), so full of the rich promises and revelations of the Messiah and His kingdom. By quoting this opening prophecy of himself, the Baptist announces by implication the approaching fulfilment of the whole section.
1:24: 24. The whole deputation (not a new delegation) had been sent from the Pharisees — a detail which may explain the character of the following question about baptism, since the Pharisees were the most precise about all ceremonies and lustrations.
1:25: 25. The question 'Why baptizest thou, if thou art none of these?' shows probably that the deputation did not interpret Isa. xl. 3 as referring to any herald of the Messiah. They regarded baptism as a significant token of the approach of the Messianic Kingdom, and asked: Why do you so act, if you hold no forerunner's office?
1:26:
26, 27. μέσος ὑμῶν ἕστηκεν ὃν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε — He who comes after me stands among you. The subject of the sentence is ὁ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος. The insertions found in some manuscripts have been made by scribes unaware of this construction and wishing to harmonize the verse with vv. 15 and 30. The Baptist's declaration that the Messiah was standing among them at that moment unknown to them was an answer to their challenge demanding a legitimation of his prophetic claims — a σημεῖον that he was sent from God (compare ch. ii. 18).

οὗ οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐγὼ ἄξιος ἵνα λύσω αὐτοῦ τὸν ἱμάντα τοῦ ὑποδήματος — see note on Matt. iii. 11.
1:28: 28. Βηθανίᾳ beyond Jordan: this is the reading of nearly all manuscripts, and was read by Heracleon. The reading Βηθαβαρᾷ is Origen's conjecture, based on his local investigations; he concedes that Bethany was found in almost all copies. That no Bethany beyond Jordan was known in his time proves but little: three hundred eventful years had changed the face of Palestine since these events, and the names of many obscure places had been forgotten.
1:29:
vv. 29–34. Second witness borne by John to Jesus: apparently before his disciples.

29. τῇ ἐπαύριον — the day after, literally. Those who wish to insert the Temptation between vv. 28 and 29 interpret it 'on some day after,' but this sense is not according to the usage of John (see refs.), and would be quite alien from the precision of this whole portion of the narrative, which specifies even the hours of the day (ver. 39).

ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου — one of the most important and difficult sayings in the NT. The title must refer to some known and particular lamb. (α) The paschal lamb? The dominant idea in the paschal sacrifice has no connexion with αἴρειν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν: no mention of sin or its removal occurs in any Jewish connexion with the paschal lamb. (β) The daily sacrifice? Too general and miscellaneous a reference; and the lamb was never used for a sin-offering properly so called. (γ) There remains but one reference: the prophetic announcement of Isa. liii. 7. The whole latter section of Isaiah is Messianic. There alone is the connexion between the lamb and the bearing/taking away of sin expressly stated — see Isa. liii. 4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 12. I have therefore no doubt that this was the reference.

ὁ αἴρων = αἴρειν answers to the Hebrew נָשָׂא, used with חֵטְא or עָוֺן in the sense of bearing the burden of sin and taking it away by expiation.
1:30: 30. See on ver. 15. The earlier testimony — uttered before the Baptist saw Jesus in the flesh — is now formally identified with this particular person who stood before him.
1:31: 31. κἀγὼ οὐκ ᾔδειν αὐτόν — this is entirely consistent with the supposition that John had been from youth acquainted with our Lord and may even have believed Him to be the Christ: but having (ver. 33) a special sign appointed him by which to recognize Him as Messiah, until that sign was given he — like the rest of the people (κἀγώ, ver. 26) — had no certain knowledge of Him. De Wette gives the sense well: 'This testimony does not rest upon my long personal acquaintance with Him, but on what happened during my work of baptizing.'
1:32:
32, 33. The occurrence related here happened at the baptism of Jesus, which is presupposed as known. τεθέαμαι (perfect) — 'I have seen,' with present force, in reference to the sign divinely intimated to him, in the abiding fulfilment of which he now stood.

ἔμεινεν ἐπ᾽ αὐτόν — by some appearance not further described, the Holy Spirit was manifested to John as not removing from Jesus again, but abiding on Him. The gift of the Holy Spirit did not ordinarily accompany John's baptism (ch. vi. 39: Acts i. 5; xix. 2 ff.), but only in this one case; its occurrence was to point out the Messiah. As to the account: the appearance was confined to the Lord and the Baptist — he was to receive the sign, and then testify to others (κατά τινα πνευματικὴν θεωρίαν ὤφθη μόνῳ τῷ Ἰωάννῃ, Theod. Mops.).

The Personal Logos, who σὰρξ ἐγένετο and was subjected to all the laws of human development, was the Recipient (τὸ δεχόμενον) of this fulness of the indwelling Holy Ghost: and herein consisted the real depth of the sign — the abiding of the Spirit without measure (ch. iii. 34) indicated beyond doubt that He was the λόγος σὰρξ γεγονώς; for no mere human intelligence could be thus receptive of the Holy Spirit of God, who is received by men only by measure, according to our capacities.
1:34: 34. A solemn reiteration of his testimony after the mention of the giving of this token by Him who sent him. μεμαρτύρηκα is stronger than μαρτυρῶ — a reference to his testimony as a thing on record in their memories, and as still continuing. ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ (see ver. 18) = the Logos made flesh, the Messiah.
1:35:
vv. 35–43. On account of the testimony of John, first Andrew and another of his disciples, and through Andrew, Simon Peter, become acquainted with Jesus.

35. τῇ ἐπαύριον — see on ver. 29. The two disciples had probably been present on the preceding day; what they then heard had made a powerful impression, so that the repetition of the testimony is now the signal for them to follow Jesus.
1:36: 36. The second utterance of the same testimony: ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. See on ver. 29.
1:37: 37. ἠκολούθησαν must not be understood in the narrower apostolic sense of leaving all to follow Him; here it is only of mechanically going after Him, βουλόμενοι πεῖραν λαβεῖν αὐτοῦ — wishing to make trial of Him (Euthymius).
1:38: 38. τί ζητεῖτε; — not from ignorance (He who searches the thoughts of men), but to draw them out and set them at ease. They must have been hesitating and constrained as strangers. ποῦ μένεις; — they enquire after His lodging, intending to visit Him in private and with leisure (Euthymius). Perhaps He was then apparently going thither, as it was late in the day. But He furthers their wish by inviting them to follow.
1:39: 39. ὡς δεκάτη — about the tenth hour, i.e. 4 P.M., according to the Jewish reckoning. The Evangelist always reckons according to the Jewish method (see ch. iv. 6, 52; xix. 14 and notes). They remained with Him the rest of that day, which would be four or five hours.
1:40: 40. Andrew is identified as one of the two who followed Jesus. The other (unnamed) is most likely the Evangelist himself: (1) he never names himself in his Gospel; (2) this account bears marks of an eye-witness in its minute accuracy, specifying even the hours; (3) the name would certainly have been given if it were not suppressed for a special reason. Such has been the general opinion of commentators.
1:41: 41. εὑρίσκει οὗτος πρῶτον τὸν ἀδελφὸν τὸν ἴδιον Σίμωνα — ἴδιον is not merely the possessive pronoun, but refers to πρῶτον and furnishes a reason for it: he first sought his own brother. εὑρήκαμεν τὸν Μεσσίαν — not ὁ Χριστός (with the article, the official title) but Χριστός, the identification simply of the two words in their meaning.
1:42: 42. The first bestowal of the new name on Simon, from our Lord's prophetic knowledge of his future character. See note on Matt. xvi. 18. Κηφᾶς = Aramaic, Hebrew κεφ, 'a stone.' The Greek name Peter became prevalent in the apostolic Church very soon; Paul uses both names indiscriminately. The emphatic use of ἐμβλέψας is hardly accountable except on the explanation of supernatural knowledge: 'I know who and what thou art from thy birth till thy present coming to me; I name thee, I give thee a new name, I know what I will make of thee in thy following of Me' (Stier).
1:43: 43. Here for the first time Jesus Himself calls a disciple. But ἀκολούθει does not here bear its strict apostolic sense; Philip's subsequent seeking of others, and the εὑρήκαμεν of ver. 45, unite him to the company of those who as yet were not inseparably attached as followers to Jesus.
1:44:
vv. 44–51. The calling of Philip and Nathanael.

44. τῇ ἐπαύριον — apparently the day after the naming of Peter, and therefore the fourth day after ver. 19. Jesus is on the point of setting out from the Jordan valley to Galilee. Βηθσαΐδά — Bethsaida on the western bank of the lake of Gennesareth (see note on Luke ix. 10), not Bethsaida Julias at the northern end.
1:45: 45. ὃν ἔγραψεν Μωυσῆς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ καὶ οἱ προφῆται — probably Deut. xviii. 15, but also the promises to Abraham (Gen. xvii. 7 al.), the prophecy of Jacob (Gen. xlix. 10), and the Prophets passim. τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἀπὸ Ναζαρέτ — Philip expresses what was the prevailing belief, in ordinary words. No stress can fairly be laid on this as indicating ignorance of the birth narratives in Matthew and Luke: Philip speaks as the common people spoke. Neander remarks that by combining John's declarations that in Jesus the Eternal Word became flesh (ver. 14) and that which is born of flesh is flesh (ch. iii. 6), a supernatural working of God in the conception of the Man Christ Jesus is implied.
1:46:
46. It does not appear where Nathanael was found; but he is described in ch. xxi. 2 as ὁ ἀπὸ Κανᾶ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, so the call may have taken place near Cana. Nathanael is mentioned only in these two places; as he is nowhere found in the catalogues of the Twelve but Philip is consistently associated with Bartholomew, it has been supposed that Nathanael and Bartholomew were the same person — though this is mere conjecture.

It is impossible that Nathanael, himself a Galilæan, could speak from any contempt for Galilee generally: we have no evidence that Nazareth was held in contempt among the Galilæans. He alluded therefore to the smallness and insignificance of the town in proportion to the great things now predicated of it. Nazareth is never named in the OT nor in Josephus.
1:47: 47. ἀληθῶς Ἰσραηλίτης, ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἔστιν — 'an Israelite who truly answers to the inner and honourable meaning of the name.' When we reflect what was contained in that name, and who it is that speaks, we can hardly agree with De Wette that the words are spoken merely in the spirit in which every nation attaches peculiar virtues to itself. Our Lord probably referred to Ps. xv.
1:48:
48. πρὸ τοῦ σε Φίλιππον φωνῆσαι ὄντα ὑπὸ τὴν συκήν, εἶδόν σε — the Evangelist certainly intends a supernatural insight by the Lord into Nathanael's character. The remark was overheard (the place was not now in sight) and immediately recognized as indicating perfect knowledge. To suppose that Jesus merely overheard Nathanael's question (De Wette), or that εἶδόν σε means only 'I knew thy character at first sight from a distance' (Lücke), is to make the conviction expressed in ver. 49 unaccountable.

ὄντα ὑπὸ τὴν συκήν (Wordsworth): 'is something more than ὑπὸ τῇ συκῇ — the accusative indicates retirement thither as well as concealment there — perhaps for purposes of prayer and meditation.' It contains in it, 'when thou wentest under the fig-tree, and while thou wert there.'
1:49: 49. σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, σὺ βασιλεὺς εἶ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ — Nathanael's confession. Olshausen maintains that ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ was not a Jewish appellation for the Messiah. But it was not for the mere use of this name that the Jews took up stones (ch. x. 33), but for using it in a close and literal sense — ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν — which was unintelligible and appeared blasphemous to them. The name was certainly not so common as 'Son of David,' and Nathanael can hardly have meant it in other than its popular Messianic meaning; the synonymous and better-known appellation βασιλεὺς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ which he adds confirms this.
1:50: 50. ὅτι εἶπόν σοι ὅτι εἶδόν σε ὑποκάτω τῆς συκῆς, πιστεύεις; Our Lord says this not in blame but in praise of the simple and honest expression of Nathanael's conviction; yet principally to show him that if he believed on account of this comparatively small proof of His divine power, his faith would increase from strength to strength at the greater proofs which should from that time forward be given. Compare ch. xvi. 31 and xx. 29.
1:51:
51. ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν — the double Amen is peculiar to John. Stier remarks that 'the Verily, verily, I say unto you of the Lord is spoken in His coequality with the Father: not as the Thus saith the Lord of the Prophets.' ὑμῖν (plural) — the words following are spoken to all the disciples present, not to Nathanael only.

ὄψεσθε τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα, καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — it is not the outward visible opening of the material heavens, nor the literal ascent and descent of angels in the sight of men, which our Lord here announces; but the series of glories about to be unfolded in His Person and Work from that time forward. Luther says beautifully: 'When Christ became man and had entered on His ministerial office and begun to preach, then was the heaven opened, and remains open; and has from that time never been shut, and never will be shut, although we do not see it with our bodily eyes.' The words have a plain reference to the ladder of Jacob (Gen. xxviii. 12) and imply that what Jacob then saw was now to receive its fulfilment: that He, the Son of Man, was the dwelling of God and the gate of Heaven, and that through Him, and on Him in the first place, was to descend all communication of help and grace from above.

τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — an expression originally derived, in its Messianic sense, from Dan. vii. 13, 14, and thenceforward used as one of the titles of the Messiah. It is never predicated of our Lord by any but Himself, except in Acts vii. 56 (Stephen, in apparent allusion to Matt. xxvi. 64) and in the passages of the Revelation (ch. i. 13; xiv. 14) which are almost citations from Daniel.
